title: Put on love (Colossians 3:12–17)
hookLine: clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, patience
tomorrow: what does faith look like in a pair of old work gloves?

lines: DRESSED FOR WHO YOU'RE TRYING TO BE.
cards: Some mornings people dress for who they're trying to be: the interview shirt, the running shoes not yet worn. Is that fake, or a start? Is a kind word you don't feel yet a lie, or a first step?
Christians argue about that very question with today's verses. Paul has just told the Colossians to take off anger and lying like old clothes.
Now he opens the wardrobe: "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering."

teach.b: Bowels of mercies is the old way of saying compassion felt in the gut.
Then the hardest piece: "Forbearing one another, and forgiving one another, if any man have a quarrel against any: even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye."

And the top layer: "And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness." Charity here is love, the bond that holds the outfit together. So can love be put on before it's felt?
Two views, both inside the faith. The first says yes.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: PUT IT ON, IT SHAPES YOU.
teach.b: In this passage love is something done: forbear, forgive.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: BELOVED FIRST, THEN CLOTHES.
teach.b: Put the clothes on, and over time they shape the one wearing them. Wait for the feeling, and you may wait forever. The second says slow down and look at the order.
Holy and beloved comes before a single garment. The clothes come after being loved, not in place of it.

Skip that, and love can turn into a performance, a smile over a grudge. Both are reading the same verse. And both keep this: love goes on last, over everything, and nobody wears these clothes alone in a room.
Then the scene widens: the peace of God ruling in the heart, and a church "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs." Love, it turns out, also gets sung.

how: Colossians 3:12–17 is a reading some couples choose for their weddings, and some Christians use the list of virtues as a short morning check.

o: love worn over every other virtue, holding them together
a polite smile worn so nobody sees you're upset
a warm feeling that arrives on its own, or not at all

p: love, the bond of the rest

s: Paul lists love as one virtue among many, in no special place
"above all these things put on charity": love goes on last, over everything.
'charity' in this verse means giving money
here charity is love, the bond that holds the other virtues together.
"if any man have a quarrel against any": he plans for it, and asks for forgiving.

games.q: you think love can be put on before it's felt. your friend says that's just a costume. what's the strongest version of her view, from the verse?
o: the clothes come after 'holy and beloved'; skip that, and love can become a performance.
Paul never mentions feelings at all, so love is only about how things look.
Paul says to wait until the anger is gone before trying to be kind.
games.why: her best case is in the order of the verse: beloved first, then the garments. yours is in the verbs: forbear, forgive, put on. both are reading the same lines.

practice: Touch the things you're wearing one at a time, slowly: a sleeve, a collar, a shoe. With each one, name a word from Paul's list, kindness, meekness, patience, and with the last one, love.
Go slowly enough that each word gets a breath of its own, and if someone who'll test your patience today comes to mind, let the last layer go on over them too.

wordCard.voice: Put on love. The last layer in Colossians three: love over compassion, kindness and patience, the bond that holds them together.

orig.note: Greek: bond, something that binds together, in Colossians 3:14.

carryVoice: The line to keep: above all, love, put on by people already called beloved. Rest well.
